originalFindings.claim: FunctionRegistry._populate_function_table() mutates and re-shares the base class's FUNCTION_TABLE dict object across all Functions subclasses, so registering custom functions via one Functions subclass (the documented mechanism for the public options.custom_functions API) leaks those functions into the base jmespath.functions.Functions class and into every other, unrelated Functions subclass defined afterward. This breaks the expected isolation of separately configured custom-function extensions: an application that defines its own CustomFunctions subclass for use with jmespath.search(expr, data, options=Options(custom_functions=...)) will, as a side effect of the class body executing, silently add its function names to the base Functions.FUNCTION_TABLE dict (since Python class creation calls the metaclass __init__ immediately on import/definition, not on instantiation). Consequently: (1) plain jmespath.functions.Functions() instances (used when no options/custom_functions are supplied) gain the ability to call functions they were never meant to expose, and (2) if a second, independent Functions subclass is defined in the same process (e.g. by a different library or another part of the app), it inherits functions registered by the first, and vice versa, because getattr(cls, 'FUNCTION_TABLE', {}) returns the inherited dict *object* by reference (not a copy) whenever the subclass has not yet set its own FUNCTION_TABLE class attribute, and the subsequent in-place mutation (function_table[name[6:]] = ...) followed by cls.FUNCTION_TABLE = function_table therefore mutates the shared/base dict too.

FunctionRegistry._populate_function_table mutates a FUNCTION_TABLE dict that is shared by reference across sibling/ancestor Functions subclasses when a subclass does not explicitly declare its own `FUNCTION_TABLE = {}`. Because `getattr(cls, 'FUNCTION_TABLE', {})` performs normal attribute lookup, it returns the identical dict object inherited from the base `Functions` class (or another already-defined ancestor/sibling) rather than a fresh copy. The subsequent `function_table[name[6:]] = {...}` mutations therefore write into that shared dict, and `cls.FUNCTION_TABLE = function_table` merely re-binds the same shared object onto the new subclass. Consequence: (1) custom functions registered in one Functions subclass leak into the base `jmespath.functions.Functions.FUNCTION_TABLE` and into any other independently-defined Functions subclass that also omits its own FUNCTION_TABLE declaration; (2) a `jmespath.search()` call configured with `options=Options(custom_functions=CustomFunctionsA())` can successfully invoke a function (`my_func_b`) that was only ever defined on an unrelated class `CustomFunctionsB`, meaning per-instance/per-class function isolation promised by the public custom-function extension API is not honored. This is a defect in scope because the task explicitly asks to evaluate whether separately configured function extensions preserve expected behavior, including inherited functions -- and this shows they leak across separately configured extensions rather than being properly isolated or properly inherited.

originalFindings.claim: relative(from, to) treats Windows drive letters ('C:', 'D:') as ordinary path segments rather than distinct filesystem roots. When 'from' and 'to' resolve to different drives, the common-prefix-stripping loop in relative() immediately breaks on the first segment mismatch (drive letter vs drive letter) without detecting that the two paths are on unrelated volumes, then prepends one '..' per segment of 'from' (including the drive-letter segment itself) to the segments of 'to' (including its drive-letter segment). For from='C:\\foo', to='D:\\bar' this produces '../../D:/bar' instead of Node's actual win32 behavior, which returns the 'to' path unchanged ('D:\\bar') because relative paths cannot cross drive roots. The nonsensical '..' segments would, if resolved back with resolve()/join() from 'C:/foo', walk above the drive root into '..' and '../..' rather than landing on 'D:/bar', so the returned value is not usable as a correct relative path between the two locations.

originalFindings.claim: resolve() (and therefore relative(), which is built on resolve()) does not implement the UNC/device-path preservation that normalize() explicitly implements, so resolving a UNC or `//./` device path silently drops or corrupts the leading double-slash marker instead of preserving it. normalize() detects `_UNC_REGEX` and explicitly re-adds `//` (or `//./`) before returning, but resolve() only checks `isAbsolute(resolvedPath)` and prepends a single `/`, and its `isAbsolute` check itself excludes the `//.` device form (`^[/\\]{2}(?!\.)`), so such paths fail the absolute check entirely and get concatenated with `cwd()` as if they were relative. Verified: normalize("//server/share/a") correctly returns "//server/share/a", but resolve("//server/share/a") returns "/server/share/a" (one slash lost, changing a network-share reference into an unrelated root-local path). More severely, normalize("//./c:/temp/file") correctly returns "//./c:/temp/file", but resolve("//./c:/temp/file") returns "/source/c:/temp/file" (cwd of the probe container) - the device-UNC path is treated as relative and merged with the current working directory, producing a completely different, nonsensical path. Since relative() computes `resolve(from)` and `resolve(to)` internally, any relative() call involving UNC/device-style Windows paths inherits this corruption (e.g. relative("//server/share/a","//server/share/b") returns "../b", which happens to look plausible only because both operands lose the marker identically, but the loss of the UNC prefix is itself an information-losing, silently wrong transformation compared to normalize()'s documented/tested support for the same input forms).
